title: Beatrix and the Atlas
premise: In the waning months of the Republic of Vessany, Beatrix Okafor serves as a courier carrying the Atlas—a ledger holding the names of every citizen promised evacuation before the invading army arrives. When soldiers requisition the river town of Callowmere and seize the Atlas, Beatrix discovers the ledger is incomplete: their own found family, the ragged household at the old atlas-maker's shop, was never entered. To restore the names means forging a state document and betraying the oath of neutrality that has kept them invisible; to leave it means choosing, from twenty-two people, who gets the last berth on the final barge. Beatrix forges the Atlas, is caught, and at the climax trades their own berth and confession to save the others. The family escapes; Beatrix remains behind, and in the final chapter, years later, a letter arrives proving they survived—and that the forged Atlas became the republic's true record of who it was.
about_author: Jude Vasquez is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing displaced-persons records before turning to fiction. They write from a canal-side flat in Ghent, where they keep an unfinished atlas of towns that no longer exist.

chapters.title: The Weight of Paper
chapters.summary: Beatrix Okafor, POV. In the atlas-maker's shop that doubles as a courier post, Beatrix copies dispatches and reflects on a life built on being unremarkable. The household—six found-family members—argues over supper about rumors of war. Beat: the comfort of chosen routine, and the first hairline crack in it.

chapters.title: What the River Brings
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Beatrix is summoned to collect the Atlas, the ledger of evacuation names, from a dying government clerk who warns that the army is three days out. The clerk's fear unsettles Beatrix's belief that history happens elsewhere. Beat: dread arriving by boat, wrapped in oilcloth.

chapters.title: The Requisition
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Soldiers in grey occupy Callowmere's square and commandeer the atlas-maker's shop for a signals office. Beatrix hides the Atlas inside a hollowed folio. The household pretends to be servants to avoid registration. Beat: the moment invisibility stops being a choice and becomes a performance.

chapters.title: Names We Were Never Given
chapters.summary: Marisol, the household's cook and matriarch, POV. Marisol recalls how each member of the family arrived—deserters, orphans, a disgraced cartographer—and realizes none of their names are in the Atlas. She says nothing at first. Beat: the quiet horror of being officially nobody, and love that predates paperwork.

chapters.title: The Berth Count
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Beatrix confirms the final barge leaves in nine days with exactly one berth unclaimed by priority. They begin, guiltily, to count the household against the number. Beat: the corrosive arithmetic of survival, and the first lie told to Marisol's face.

chapters.title: Captain Ilves
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. The occupying captain, Ilves, proves neither brute nor fool; he quotes poetry and suspects the shop hides more than maps. He offers Beatrix a bargain: cooperation in exchange for protection. Beat: the seduction of safety offered by the very power destroying everything.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Fingernails
chapters.summary: Tomas, the disgraced cartographer, POV. Tomas discovers the Atlas's security watermark and realizes it can be forged with the shop's own plates. He and Beatrix argue half the night about whether saving everyone justifies betraying the courier's oath. Beat: loyalty to a dead republic versus loyalty to the living.

chapters.title: The Festival They Cancel
chapters.summary: Marisol, POV. The army cancels the town's harvest festival, but Marisol holds a secret one in the cellar—candles, stolen wine, a song. For one night the household is simply a family. Beat: joy as defiance, and the reader's knowledge that it cannot last.

chapters.title: A Name Entered
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Testing the forgery, Beatrix enters a single real name—Marisol's—into the Atlas. The ink takes perfectly, and Beatrix is shaken by how easy it was. Ilves nearly catches them at the signals desk. Beat: the point of no return crossed in a single stroke of the pen.

chapters.title: The Informant
chapters.summary: Petra, the youngest household member, POV. Petra, who has been running errands for the soldiers for extra bread, realizes she has seen the shop's cellar and could be made to talk. She confesses to Beatrix in terror. Beat: innocence weaponized by circumstance, and Beatrix's protective fury.

chapters.title: Twenty-Two Names
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Beatrix forges all twenty-two names into the Atlas in one feverish night, Tomas inking the watermark, Marisol keeping watch. It is beautiful and criminal. Beat: the family united in a single act of treason, and the terrible calm that follows.

chapters.title: Audit
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Ilves announces a document audit; every ledger in the signals office will be verified against central records in four days—two days before the barge. He watches Beatrix too long as he says it. Beat: the trap closing, and the suspicion that Ilves already knows.

chapters.title: What Marisol Knew
chapters.summary: Marisol, POV. Marisol reveals she has known about the forgery since the first night and kept silent—she has buried two families already and will not bury this one. She tells Beatrix to take the berth and go. Beat: a mother's love expressed as a command Beatrix cannot obey.

chapters.title: The Cartographer's Confession
chapters.summary: Tomas, POV. Tomas admits the forged watermark has a flaw only an expert would catch, and that Ilves trained as a surveyor. The family realizes the audit is a hunt with one target: them. Beat: the plan's fatal flaw, and Tomas's guilt at having built the trap's teeth.

chapters.title: Smoke Over Callowmere
chapters.summary: Petra, POV. The army burns the eastern quarter as a 'sanitary measure.' The household shelters neighbors in the cellar; the town's invisibility is over for everyone now. Beat: private stakes made public, and Petra's transformation from frightened child to witness.

chapters.title: The Bargain Refused
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Ilves offers Beatrix everything—safe passage, the family spared—if Beatrix surrenders the forged Atlas and testifies that the republic's records were falsified from the start. Beatrix refuses, and Ilves, almost regretful, orders the audit moved up to tomorrow. Beat: the climax's trigger, and mutual respect between enemies.

chapters.title: The Night of Ink and Water
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. The family attempts to steal the Atlas back before the audit. The signals office alarm rises; Tomas is shot covering the escape; Beatrix gets the ledger to the river but Ilves intercepts them on the quay. Beat: the climax's first blow—victory and catastrophe in the same breath.

chapters.title: One Berth
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. Ilves offers a final trade: the Atlas returned, the family unprosecuted, one berth on the barge—in exchange for Beatrix's confession and surrender. Beatrix chooses the family over themselves, dictating a confession that names the forgery as theirs alone. Beat: the thematic heart—truth offered as the price of love, and paid gladly.

chapters.title: The Barge at Dawn
chapters.summary: Marisol, POV. The family boards through fog, counting heads and finding the count wrong by one. Marisol understands what Beatrix has done and screams at the receding quay. Beat: grief and gratitude fused—the found family made real by the one who stayed behind.

chapters.title: Interrogation
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. In a cell, Beatrix gives Ilves the confession he demanded, but also the argument they've been building for the whole book: that a republic is only the sum of the names someone bothered to write down. Ilves files the forged Atlas as authentic. Beat: quiet victory inside defeat; the enemy's small mercy.

chapters.title: The Town That Kept Its Name
chapters.summary: Petra, POV, years later. In a resettlement town across the border, the household endures—Marisol's kitchen, Tomas's one-handed maps, Petra teaching children to write their own names. A letter arrives in a familiar hand. Beat: belonging rebuilt from loss; the found family holding.

chapters.title: Beatrix and the Atlas
chapters.summary: Beatrix, POV. In a work camp hospital, Beatrix reads Marisol's reply and the news that the forged Atlas entered the new state's archives as the republic's true census—the record historians now trust. Beatrix, who believed history happened to other people, realizes they became its author. Beat: resolution—truth, loyalty, and belonging reconciled in ink.
